questions.q: Per this lesson, which native feature would you check to find out who changed a Validation Rule or a sharing setting?
options: Field History Tracking
Event Monitoring
Setup Audit Trail
The Individual object
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail specifically logs administrative/configuration changes like modifications to Validation Rules, sharing settings, and permissions.

questions.q: What is the main practical limitation of Setup Audit Trail that this lesson highlights?
options: It cannot log any configuration changes at all
It only works for custom objects, never for standard ones
It requires a separate Shield license just to view any entries
It has a short native retention window -- commonly cited around 180 days -- after which entries age out, which isn't enough for compliance regimes requiring multi-year retention
questions.explain: The lesson identifies Setup Audit Trail's short retention window (commonly cited around 180 days) as its real limitation, requiring export/archiving for any longer compliance requirement.

questions.q: What gap does Event Monitoring (Shield) close that Setup Audit Trail and Field History Tracking don't cover, per this lesson?
options: Event Monitoring captures usage events -- logins, report exports, API calls, page views -- showing access/usage patterns, not just changes, which the change-tracking features were never designed to capture
Event Monitoring is simply a longer-retention version of Field History Tracking with no other difference
Event Monitoring replaces the need for Setup Audit Trail entirely
Event Monitoring only tracks changes to Validation Rules
questions.explain: The lesson explains that viewing or exporting records without changing them is invisible to change-tracking tools -- Event Monitoring is specifically built to surface that usage/access activity.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say treating Setup Audit Trail, Field History, and Login History as one undifferentiated "audit log" causes real gaps?
options: Because they are actually the exact same feature under three different names
Because only one of the three features is ever enabled in any given org
Because combining them is technically impossible in Salesforce
Because each answers a different audit question (configuration changes, record field changes, or user activity), and relying on only one will miss the kind of event the others are designed to catch
questions.explain: The lesson's three-feature breakdown exists specifically because each covers a distinct kind of event, and checking only one leaves blind spots for the other two kinds.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the short native retention windows across Setup Audit Trail, Login History, and standard Field History Tracking force a governance decision?
options: None of them, on their own, meet multi-year compliance retention requirements, so a governance program has to deliberately decide who exports which audit data, how often, and where it's archived once it leaves Salesforce's native window
They don't require any decision, since Salesforce automatically archives everything forever by default
Because these features can only be used during a single fiscal quarter
Because compliance regulations never require more than 180 days of audit retention
questions.explain: The lesson draws a direct parallel to Lesson 6's retention-policy gap: short native windows mean a deliberate export/archive decision is required to meet longer compliance obligations.
